const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > enrichment/bible/work/s001/discovery/pilot1-20261005/1_1/luna/list.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Exod.34.6	Divine name and RḤM	The source commentary centers Allah’s name with Raḥmān/Raḥīm; Exodus has YHWH self-identify as compassionate and gracious, using the Hebrew RḤM cognate in the same divine-name formula.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Isa.49.15	Womb and compassion	The commentary links Raḥīm to the womb as a sheltering home; Isaiah asks whether a mother can withhold compassion from the child of her womb, joining the womb image to the RḤM root.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Num.6.27	Name placed on the people	The commentary treats God’s name as a mark identifying the work or creature as belonging to its bearer; the priestly blessing says God’s name is placed on Israel and blesses them.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.116.17	Thank offering with the Name	The commentary connects invoking God’s name with animal offerings; the psalmist makes a thank offering while calling on YHWH’s name, joining liturgical offering and invocation.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Gen.12.8	Calling in the Name	The source commentary’s Arabic bism means beginning an act by God’s name; Abram builds an altar and calls in YHWH’s name, a close Hebrew name-invocation formula.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.2.20	Aramaic name of God	The source labels Allah as the worshipped one and bismillah as name-invocation; Daniel blesses the name of God in Aramaic, using the cognate Elaha for God and linking name, praise, wisdom, and power.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.34.7	Mercy with judgment	The commentary says expansive mercy does not erase account or judgment; the continuation of the name formula says God forgives while not simply clearing guilt, holding mercy and consequence together.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Jonah.4.2	Merciful Name toward enemies	Jonah cites YHWH’s compassionate, gracious character to explain his flight from the mission; the same RḤM name formula shows mercy reaching even Nineveh, which Jonah resents.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Gen.43.14	Compassion for endangered kin	The commentary joins God’s name to mercy and kinship; Jacob asks El Shaddai to grant compassion as his sons travel into danger, with the Hebrew RḤM word directed toward brothers and family.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:1Kgs.3.26	A mother’s protective compassion	The source commentary describes mercy through the womb’s care for a helpless child; the true mother’s compassion rises for the living infant and makes her surrender him rather than see him killed.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Jer.31.20	Mercy toward a child	The commentary presents Rahīm as compassion directed to particular recipients; God speaks of Ephraim as a dear child and says divine compassion is stirred toward him, using the RḤM root.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Exod.33.19	Mercy directed by God	The commentary distinguishes mercy’s overflowing source from its particular recipients; God says mercy and grace are shown to whom God chooses, with the Hebrew RḤM cognate.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.103.13	A parent’s care for children	The commentary describes the womb as sustaining a child who cannot ask or repay; the psalm compares YHWH’s compassion to a father’s compassion for children.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Exod.34.6	The Arabic and Hebrew mercy roots	The commentary’s source label is Arabic ر ح م; Exodus uses Hebrew רַחוּם for God’s compassion. The cognate shows the attribute in its own covenantal declaration, not merely a similar sound.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.31.26	Sun and moon as objects of worship	The commentary recalls Abraham testing the rising star, moon, and sun and rejecting them when they set; Job names gazing at sun or moon in splendor as the setup for a forbidden act of worship.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.31.27	The gesture of worship	The commentary contrasts Allah’s name with a sun treated as divine; Job specifies the hand-kiss that would follow an inwardly enticed heart, making the bodily act of astral devotion explicit.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.31.28	Worship of celestial bodies as disloyalty	The commentary’s Abraham scene withdraws divine status from a setting star; Job calls sun or moon worship a denial of the God above, supplying the same reversal in an oath.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.18.24	Calling a god by name	The commentary distinguishes Allah’s name from empty names assigned to idols; Elijah makes rival groups call on their gods’ names and lets the answer by fire reveal which is truly God.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.42.8	YHWH’s name and rival idols	The commentary contrasts God’s substantial name with names assigned to powerless gods; Isaiah joins YHWH’s self-declared name to refusal to give divine glory to idols.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.10.11	Names without a creator	The commentary says idols are names assigned by people without divine warrant; Jeremiah says the gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish, contrasting them with the Creator.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.32.4	Aaron’s role in the calf	The commentary cites Aaron warning Israel that the calf is a test and that their Lord is Rahman; Exodus instead has Aaron take their gold and fashion the calf, a sharp difference in the same episode.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.32.19	Moses breaks the tablets	The commentary describes Moses returning angry from the calf and throwing down the tablets; Exodus narrates the same action when Moses sees the calf and the dancing.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Exod.32.24	Who made the calf	The commentary presents Aaron warning the people against the calf while Moses challenges him; Exodus has Aaron explain that he cast the gold into the fire and the calf came out, assigning Aaron a different role.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.7.7	Who enters the ark	The commentary stresses that Noah’s son refuses the ark and that safety is not inherited by blood; Genesis lists Noah, his sons, and their wives entering, without an estranged son in the passenger scene.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.7.16	God shuts the ark	The commentary places the voyage and its beginning under God’s name and mercy; Genesis says YHWH shut Noah in, making divine protection rather than Noah’s invocation the explicit safeguard.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.8.4	The ark comes to rest	The commentary unpacks Noah’s phrase for the ark’s movement and anchoring as a whole journey under God’s name; Genesis narrates the ark resting on the mountains of Ararat after the flood.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.8.20	An altar after the voyage	The commentary pairs Noah’s embarkation formula with praise and a request for a blessed landing; after leaving the ark, Genesis has Noah build an altar and offer burnt offerings.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Rosh Hashanah 17b	The thirteen attributes as prayer	The commentary begins with God’s name and mercy; the Talmud reads Exodus 34:6–7 as a ritual order of divine attributes that Israel can recite when seeking forgiveness.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Berakhot 32a	Praise before petition	The commentary reads the Fātiḥa’s opening name as leading into praise, service, and request for guidance; the Talmud says prayer should begin with praise of God before petition.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.51.19	Sacrifice and the inward offering	The commentary says animal flesh and blood do not reach God, but piety does; the psalm says God’s desired sacrifice is a broken and contrite spirit, distinguishing inward devotion from ritual material.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hosea.6.6	Mercy over sacrifice	The commentary treats sacrifice as meaningful only under God’s name and with piety; Hosea says God desires steadfast love rather than sacrifice, giving the ethical quality priority over the offering.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.6	The proposed burnt offering	The commentary contrasts the animal’s meat and blood with the worshipper’s piety; Micah begins by asking whether burnt offerings and year-old calves can satisfy God.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.7	Thousands of rams do not suffice	The commentary says sacrificial quantity is not what reaches God; Micah escalates to thousands of rams and rivers of oil, then even a firstborn, exposing the insufficiency of material offering.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.8	What God actually requires	The commentary identifies piety rather than meat or blood as what reaches God; Micah answers the sacrifice questions with justice, covenant love, and walking humbly with God.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Sam.15.22	Obedience over offerings	The commentary makes the worshipper’s God-conscious piety decisive; Samuel says listening to YHWH is better than sacrifice and obedience better than sacrificial fat.

strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.34.9	Pardon and covenant presence	After declaring the compassionate divine name, Moses asks God to go among Israel, pardon its iniquity, and take it as an inheritance; this makes mercy an active covenantal presence.

const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > enrichment/bible/work/s001/discovery/pilot1-20261005/1_1/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.34.9	Pardon and covenant presence	After declaring the compassionate divine name, Moses asks God to go among Israel, pardon its iniquity, and take it as an inheritance; this makes mercy an active covenantal presence.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:1Kgs.8.50	Compassion for captives	Solomon asks God to forgive exiles and grant them compassion before their captors, using the RḤM root; this makes Rahīm protection concrete for a vulnerable people.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.30.3	Compassion gathers the exiles	The commentary describes mercy as shelter and as directed care; Moses promises that after exile God will have compassion on Israel and gather the scattered, using the RḤM root.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:2Sam.24.14	Mercy as refuge	David chooses to fall into YHWH’s hand because divine mercies are great, rather than into human hands; this links RḤM mercy to the protection and refuge described in the commentary.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.124.8	Help in the Name	The commentary connects Rahman’s name with the Fātiḥa’s request for help; the psalm says Israel’s help is in YHWH’s name, the maker of heaven and earth.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.18.10	The Name as a safe place	The commentary puts the ark and the womb under the protection of God’s name and mercy; Proverbs says YHWH’s name is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are safe.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.12.5	The place where God’s Name dwells	The commentary links animals offered at the House with the name spoken over them; Deuteronomy sends Israel to the place God chooses to make his name dwell.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.12.6	Offerings brought to the named place	The commentary describes animals separated from the herd and brought to the House under God’s name; Deuteronomy lists sacrifices and firstlings brought to the place chosen for YHWH’s name.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.22.13	A ram offered in place of a son	The commentary considers the status of sacrificial animals and their relation to God; in the binding of Isaac, Abraham offers a ram instead of his son, making the animal’s offering inseparable from a threatened life.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.1.11	God rejects offerings without right conduct	The commentary says meat and blood do not reach God while piety does; Isaiah has God reject abundant burnt offerings in a community whose worship is disconnected from justice.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.1.16	The worshipper must change	The commentary locates the value of offering in the worshipper’s piety; Isaiah turns from rejected sacrifices to washing, ceasing evil, and cleansing conduct.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.1.17	Piety shown as justice	The commentary says what reaches God is not sacrificial flesh but the worshipper’s God-consciousness; Isaiah specifies justice for the oppressed, orphan, and widow as the required response.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.5.22	Offerings rejected at judgment	The commentary subordinates sacrificial material to piety; Amos says God will not accept Israel’s burnt offerings and grain offerings in a community facing judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.5.24	Justice instead of cultic display	The commentary makes devotion visible in the worshipper rather than the animal’s flesh and blood; Amos follows rejected offerings with a demand that justice flow like water.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Berakhot 6:1	Blessing before eating	The commentary says invoking God’s name changes the status of food; the Mishnah prescribes a blessing before eating different kinds of food, a Jewish table practice that places ordinary eating under God’s name.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Berakhot 35a	Enjoyment requires a blessing	The commentary connects God’s name to whether food may be eaten; the Talmud says one may not benefit from the world without a blessing, directly linking invocation to eating.
strong	tevrat	soydas	Sirach 2:11	The Lord’s merciful name	The commentary’s Raḥmān and Raḥīm name God’s mercy and forgiveness; Sirach says the Lord is compassionate and merciful, forgives sins, and saves in distress.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 18:13	Mercy toward all living beings	The commentary distinguishes overflowing mercy from its direction to recipients; Sirach contrasts human compassion for a neighbor with the Lord’s compassion for all living beings and a shepherd’s care for the flock.
strong	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 11:23	Mercy over all creation	The commentary says divine mercy encompasses everything; Wisdom says God has mercy on all because God can do all things and patiently allows sinners to repent.
strong	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 11:26	Creation belongs to its merciful Lord	The commentary links the name with mercy toward creatures; Wisdom says God spares all because all are God’s, adding belonging to universal mercy.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Neh.9.17	Mercy after the ancestors’ rebellion	The commentary holds mercy together with judgment; Nehemiah’s communal confession recalls rebellion and calls God ready to pardon, gracious, and merciful, using the RḤM formula.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Joel.2.13	Returning to the merciful God	The commentary describes expansive mercy that does not erase moral reckoning; Joel uses the compassionate-name formula to call Israel to return, with God’s relenting from calamity as the hoped-for response.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:2Chr.30.9	Mercy for the returning remnant	The commentary says Rahīm turns toward particular people; Hezekiah promises that returning exiles’ kin may find compassion because YHWH is gracious and merciful and will not turn away.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.4.31	Mercy that keeps covenant	The commentary joins mercy to God’s name and care for those under it; Moses says YHWH is a merciful God who will not abandon Israel or forget the covenant, using the RḤM root.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Sam.17.45	A deed begun in YHWH’s Name	The commentary says the speaker puts God’s name before the action; David tells Goliath that he comes against him in the name of YHWH, making the name the declared authority for a concrete deed.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.1.49	The holy Name in praise	The commentary opens with God’s name and leads into praise; Mary’s song says the Mighty One has done great things and his name is holy, placing the Name in a liturgical act of thanksgiving.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.1.50	Mercy from generation to generation	The commentary joins God’s name with mercy; Mary’s song immediately describes mercy extending through generations to those who fear God, making the two themes part of one praise sequence.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.28.19	Baptism into the Name	The commentary treats God’s name as a mark that identifies and claims the bearer; Jesus commands baptism into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a Christian ritual that marks belonging.
strong	incil	motif	Didache 9:5	Communion limited to the baptized in the Name	The commentary links God’s name to food’s religious status; the Didache says only the baptized into the Lord’s name may eat or drink the Eucharist, making the Name a boundary for a sacred meal.
strong	incil	motif	Didache 10:2	Thanksgiving for the holy Name at the meal	The commentary places food and praise under God’s name; the Didache’s post-meal thanksgiving blesses God for the holy Name made to dwell in believers’ hearts.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.3.6	Healing in Jesus’ Name	The commentary says the divine name accompanies a concrete action; Peter tells the lame man to walk in the name of Jesus Christ, making the Name the stated means of the act.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.2.21	Calling on the Lord’s Name for rescue	The commentary connects God’s name with seeking help and protection; Peter quotes Joel that everyone who calls on the Lord’s name will be saved, applying the invocation to deliverance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.21.9	The one who comes in the Lord’s Name	The commentary describes the Name at the threshold of a journey and cites a letter identified by sender and divine Name; the crowd welcomes Jesus with the scriptural blessing for the one who comes in the Lord’s name.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.2.5	Spiritual offerings acceptable to God	The commentary distinguishes piety from animal flesh and blood; Peter describes believers as a priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.14.17	Rain as provision and witness	The commentary reads rain and fruitful earth as signs of mercy that feed life; Paul says God gave rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness as testimony to divine goodness.
strong	incil	soydas	SBLGNT:1Cor.8.4	Idols have no divine substance	The commentary contrasts God’s living name with human-assigned empty divine names; Paul says an idol is nothing and that there is no God but one.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.13	Mercy at judgment	The commentary keeps Rahman’s mercy in view alongside the Day of Judgment; James says mercy triumphs over judgment, making mercy’s role at judgment explicit.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Rashi on Exodus 32:5	Aaron’s festival as delay	The commentary presents Harun warning Israel rather than endorsing the calf; Rashi reads Aaron’s announcement of a festival “tomorrow” as an attempt to delay the people until Moses returned, mitigating Aaron’s role in the parallel episode.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.86.15	Mercy invoked by an individual petitioner	The commentary describes Rahīm as compassion directed toward a recipient; the psalmist calls on the merciful, gracious, patient God while asking for personal mercy and rescue.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.145.9	Compassion over all God’s works	The commentary presents Rahman’s mercy as encompassing creation; the psalm says YHWH is good to all and has compassion over all his works.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.5.23	Speech under God’s Name	The commentary says the missing verb in bismillah is supplied by the act being undertaken; Moses tells God he has spoken to Pharaoh in God’s name, a specific speech act placed under the Name.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.28.10	A people publicly identified by the Name	The commentary’s brand image makes a mark identify its bearer; Deuteronomy says the nations will see that Israel is called by YHWH’s name and fear them.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.15.5	Stars as created signs, not gods	The commentary recalls Abraham considering the star, moon, and sun as possible lords before rejecting them; Genesis has God point to the stars as a promise of descendants, giving celestial bodies a created sign-function instead of divine status.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.1.78	Mercy pictured inwardly	The commentary connects Raḥīm with the womb and bodily care; Luke speaks of the tender compassion of God using an inward-organ image, then pictures dawn visiting from on high. The Greek image is a motif, not a cognate.
medium	incil	motif	Didache 9:1	Thanksgiving over the cup	The commentary connects invocation and food; the Didache begins its Eucharistic thanksgiving over the cup, showing a communal meal opened by blessing and gratitude.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.12.1	The worshipper as a living offering	The commentary says piety, rather than meat and blood, reaches God; Paul calls believers to present their bodies as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice, making devotion itself the offering.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.13.15	Praise as a sacrifice of the lips	The commentary’s opening name leads into praise and service; Hebrews calls continual praise, confessing God’s name, a sacrifice offered through Jesus.
medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Heb.10.4	Animal blood and atonement	The commentary says sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God, while piety does; Hebrews says animal blood cannot take away sins and directs its argument toward Christ’s offering, a different account of sacrifice’s efficacy.
medium	incil	motif	Didache 9:1	Thanksgiving over the cup	The commentary connects invocation and food; the Didache begins its Eucharistic thanksgiving over the cup, showing a communal meal opened by blessing and gratitude.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.8.6	One God and one Lord	The commentary says Allah’s name identifies the sole one worthy of worship; Paul confesses one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, while distinguishing the Christian formulation.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.5.7	Mercy returned to the merciful	The commentary describes compassion as active kindness toward the vulnerable; Jesus blesses the merciful with the promise that they will receive mercy.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.9.16	Mercy not earned by human effort	The commentary says sacrificial material does not reach God but piety does; Paul’s continuation says mercy does not depend on human willing or running but on God’s mercy, a distinct account of agency and merit.
EOF",workdir:"/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation",max_output_tokens:1000});
text(r.output);
